clue.text: Paragon gets red about nothing when laid up

parts.note: ST, short for saint, a paragon of virtue
O, the figure nought
taken as written

explanation.surface: A model of virtue blushes over nothing at all while confined to bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Laid up' suggests an invalid, but here it means put away in store, as goods are laid up for later.
explanation.definitionFit: Goods laid up are kept in reserve, put by in a warehouse or cupboard for later use.

clue.text: This stone for quality : this wood for fire

explanation.surface: A pair of tips: one kind of stone tests quality, one kind of wood lights a fire.
explanation.walkthrough: Each half names a compound: add 'stone' to the answer for the assayer's test of gold's quality, add 'wood' for the tinder that catches a spark.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are compounds on the same first word: a black assaying stone tests gold's purity, and rotten tinder-wood catches a spark.

clue.text: The year pater went mad, meeting local taxes

indicators.note: going mad means losing order, so these letters are thrown into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Dad went berserk in the year the council bills arrived.
explanation.walkthrough: 'went mad' rearranges YEAR and PATER. 'The' is a link. British local taxes were once called 'rates', paid by householders to the council.
explanation.definitionFit: Before 1990 British householders paid rates, a local property tax, so someone meeting local taxes paid them.

clue.text: Eponymous little Dickensian

parts.note: the Dickens heroine whose name, with 'Little' before it, is the novel's title

explanation.surface: A small character from Dickens who gave a book its name.
explanation.walkthrough: 'little' looks like a description, but it is part of the title: Dickens's novel is named after the heroine Amy, called Little by her family.
explanation.definitionFit: Amy, the Marshalsea-born heroine of a Dickens novel, gives the book its title with 'Little' before her surname.

clue.text: Put your money on Bill he will make the complaint

parts.note: to back a horse is to put money on it
AC, short for account, a bill
taken as written

explanation.surface: Bet on Bill, the punter is told, and he will end up with something to grumble about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' reads as a man's name, but it is an account, abbreviated AC. 'Complaint' means an ailment, not a grumble.
explanation.definitionFit: A complaint is an ailment, and a sore lower spine is a common one.

clue.text: Using bad blarney perhaps to promote charity "do"

indicators.note: perhaps says these letters could be some other word, so the three words are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone sweet-talks shamelessly to drum up support for a fundraising event.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges all the letters of USING BAD BLARNEY. The sale is a fundraiser where people donate goods and buy others' donations.
explanation.definitionFit: A jumble-style fundraising sale where donors give goods and others pay for them is a classic charitable event.

clue.text: Firm's Customs lodges under one roof

parts.note: CO, short for company, a firm
habits are customs, things regularly done

explanation.surface: A business's customs service shares a building with another office.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Customs' looks like the excise office, but it means habits. 'Lodges' is a verb: lives together.
explanation.definitionFit: To live together in one dwelling, especially as a couple, is to share a roof.

clue.text: Don't start the fire, it will damage the range

indicators.note: damaging the word knocks its letters out of order, so range is rearranged

explanation.surface: A warning about the kitchen stove: lighting it will harm the range.
explanation.walkthrough: 'range' reads as the old kitchen stove, where a fire is lit, but it is the anagram fodder that 'will damage' rearranges; 'the fire' means fury.
explanation.definitionFit: Fire is a figure for fury, a hot temper that flares up.

clue.text: Convenient headgear, say, for the races

indicators.note: say means what follows is spoken, so the phrase is heard rather than spelt

parts.note: convenient is handy and headgear is caps

explanation.surface: Handy hats for a day at the racecourse.
explanation.walkthrough: Spoken, HANDY CAPS sounds like the answer. 'Races' means events where runners carry weight or start apart to even the field.
explanation.definitionFit: Events in which better horses carry extra weight are races of that particular kind, run to level the contest.

clue.text: Flatter a pretty girl — it'll take a few pats

parts.note: to butter someone up is to flatter them
dish is old slang for an attractive girl

explanation.surface: Sweet-talk a lovely girl and she'll get a few affectionate pats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pats' reads as affectionate touches, but they are pats of butter, small portions served at the table.
explanation.definitionFit: A tableware piece that holds pats, small moulded portions of spread, for serving.

clue.text: Familiarly sounding medal

parts.note: slang for a decoration, the same word as a struck metal disc that rings out

explanation.surface: A decoration that rings out, informally speaking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Familiarly' means in slang: British servicemen call a medal by the name of the resonant metal disc struck at mealtimes, which is what 'sounding' points to.
explanation.definitionFit: Informal British slang for a medal or decoration borrows the name of a struck, resonating metal disc.

clue.text: Axing many engaged in the Scotch game

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, many
hopscotch players spend the game moving on one foot

explanation.surface: Lots of people cut down while playing a playground game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scotch game' is hopscotch, the playground game of hopping through chalked squares; to be engaged in it is to be hopping.
explanation.definitionFit: Axing is cutting with blows of a blade, as when splitting logs.

clue.text: Sir James could go right to the fence

indicators.note: letting the letter go means it is dropped from the word

parts.note: a barrier is a fence

explanation.surface: A knighted gentleman might walk straight up to the fence.
explanation.walkthrough: Read backwards, the clue says the answer plus R makes BARRIER; so 'could go' drops R from the fence. Sir James Barrie wrote Peter Pan.
explanation.definitionFit: The Scottish playwright of Peter Pan, knighted in 1913, was Sir James Matthew of that surname.

clue.text: " Don't go ", said Herrick to the daffodils

explanation.surface: The poet pleads with his spring flowers not to leave.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert Herrick's poem 'To Daffodils' begins 'Fair daffodils, we weep to see / You haste away so soon' and pleads with them to remain.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are pleas to remain: an everyday request not to leave and the plea Herrick's poem repeats to the fading flowers.

clue.text: Spinner Tom is a superior person

parts.note: a top is a toy that spins
Mark Twain's boy hero Tom has this surname

explanation.surface: The boy who spins is a cut above everyone else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spinner Tom' reads as one person, but it is two pieces. The term comes from the saw-pit, where the man on top guided the saw while another stood below.
explanation.definitionFit: In a saw-pit the sawyer standing above was the senior hand, so the term came to mean a leading or distinguished person.

clue.text: Grand race, or a member of it

explanation.surface: A famous steeplechase, or one of its runners.
explanation.walkthrough: The Grand National is Britain's great steeplechase at Aintree. 'It' slyly points back to the nation hidden in that name, whose citizen is the second sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Aintree's Grand steeplechase goes by this word alone, and a citizen of a country is one of its people.

clue.text: Beaten down or chaired across?

explanation.surface: Is the winner crushed, or carried shoulder-high over the field?
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense splits the word: to be chaired is to be borne aloft, and across is over, so it is 'borne over'.
explanation.definitionFit: Overwhelmed or suppressed means beaten down, and a person chaired across a room is carried over it.

clue.text: The better horse perhaps, but ridden to death in Devon

explanation.surface: A fine horse, though ridden till it dropped in the West Country.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb says this horse is the better one, meaning the wife rules the house; in the Devon folk song 'Widecombe Fair' Tom Pearce's old horse dies carrying seven riders.
explanation.definitionFit: A proverb calls a pale old female horse the better one of a pair, and the 'Widecombe Fair' song's overloaded horse dies on the way.

clue.text: Some pork, Eve ?

explanation.surface: A cut of meat, and the first woman.
explanation.walkthrough: Genesis says Eve was made from a rib taken from Adam, one he could do without.
explanation.definitionFit: A cut of pork from the ribs, and Eve as fashioned from one of Adam's ribs that he could spare.

clue.text: Venice once held "the gorgeous —— in fee"

definitions.text: Venice once held "the gorgeous —— in fee"

parts.words: Venice once held "the gorgeous —— in fee"
parts.note: a gap-fill from Wordsworth's sonnet on the fall of the Venetian Republic, naming the lands Venice once ruled

explanation.surface: A quotation recalling the Venetian Republic's former empire.
explanation.walkthrough: Wordsworth's 'On the Extinction of the Venetian Republic' opens 'Once did she hold the gorgeous ... in fee', meaning Venice owned the riches of the Orient.
explanation.definitionFit: The Orient, the lands of the rising sun whose trade Venice controlled, is the word filling Wordsworth's line.

clue.text: The inventor's need is obvious

explanation.surface: What an inventor requires is plain for all to see.
explanation.walkthrough: One sense is the legal grant protecting an invention; the other is the adjective meaning plain to see.
explanation.definitionFit: An inventor needs a legal grant of exclusive rights, and the same word as an adjective means plainly evident.

clue.text: Old china

parts.note: a former European name for the Chinese empire, not porcelain or a mate

explanation.surface: Antique porcelain, or perhaps an old friend.
explanation.walkthrough: The lower-case 'china' suggests porcelain or rhyming-slang 'china plate' for mate; it is the country, by the name Marco Polo's Europe used.
explanation.definitionFit: Medieval Europe knew northern China by a name derived from the Khitan people.

clue.text: What the precipitate made

parts.note: people who act rashly are said to make this, as in the proverb against it

explanation.surface: Sounds like a chemistry question about what the solid formed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'precipitate' suggests a chemist's solid deposit, but here it is the adjective as noun: rash people, who 'make' speed.
explanation.definitionFit: Rash, precipitate people act with undue speed, and one is said to make it.

clue.text: 1984 for instance ?

parts.note: 1984 is both a twelve-month span and the title of Orwell's novel, so it is both halves of the compound

explanation.surface: A question about Orwell's dystopia.
explanation.walkthrough: 1984 is a year and Orwell's book, so it is a 'year book' as a pun, though the real word means an annual reference volume.
explanation.definitionFit: An annual reference volume of the year's facts, here punned as a date that is also a novel.

clue.text: Storming where film actor gets emotional?

explanation.surface: An actor storms about and turns emotional during filming.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense splits the word: an actor emotes 'on set', in the studio where the film is shot.
explanation.definitionFit: An assault or storming attack is an older sense, and the studio stage where actors perform is the film's set.

clue.text: Not suitors, yet they may carry a proposal

definitions.text: Not suitors, yet they may carry a proposal

parts.words: Not suitors, yet they may carry a proposal
parts.note: a proposal here is a motion before a meeting, carried by votes in favour, not a marriage proposal

explanation.surface: Who but a lover makes a proposal?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suitors' and 'proposal' point to marriage, but the proposal is a motion in a debate, carried by the votes in favour.
explanation.definitionFit: Votes in favour carry a motion in Parliament or at a meeting.

clue.text: Loverlike but inexpert?

explanation.surface: Romantic but clumsy.
explanation.walkthrough: From Latin amator, a lover: the first sense reads the word as like a lover; the second is its usual meaning of unskilled.
explanation.definitionFit: Its Latin root means lover, so it can be read as lover-like, though its usual sense is unskilled.

clue.text: Sign of a yellow god's jealousy

definitions.text: Sign of a yellow god's jealousy

parts.words: Sign of a yellow god's jealousy
parts.note: the colour of jealousy plus a feature of the face, recalling J. Milton Hayes's monologue about the little yellow god's jewel

explanation.surface: A jealous idol gives itself away.
explanation.walkthrough: Jealousy is the 'green-eyed monster'; J. Milton Hayes's monologue 'The Green Eye of the Little Yellow God' tells of an idol's stolen jewel.
explanation.definitionFit: Jealousy is traditionally coloured green, and Hayes's yellow idol has a jewel for its eye.

clue.text: One under voting majority once, now two over

definitions.text: One under voting majority once, now two over

parts.words: One under voting majority once, now two over
parts.note: the age of majority was once ...-one and is now eighteen, so the number sits one below the old age and two above the new

explanation.surface: A riddle about voting age changing over the years.
explanation.walkthrough: 'majority' is the age of adulthood, not a winning margin: it was 21 in Britain until 1969, then 18.
explanation.definitionFit: A number one below the old adult age of twenty-one and two above today's eighteen.
